The Commerce Department's measure, released Friday, showed that the personal consumption 
expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, rose by just 0.1% from 
October. On an annual basis, it indicated a 2.4% inflation rate, still above the Fed’s 2% target, but lower 
than the 2.5% forecast from Dow Jones. The monthly increase was also 0.1 percentage point below 
expectations. Excluding food and energy, core PCE also rose 0.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-
over-year, both 0.1 percentage point lower than anticipated. The Fed generally views the core PCE as a 
more reliable measure of long-term inflation trends since it excludes the more volatile categories of 
food and energy. 
COMMENTARY: The FED's preferred inflation gauge came in lower than expected, potentially easing 
some of the market's disappointment following the FED’s interest rate decision on Wednesday. The 
report was released just two days after the central bank lowered its benchmark interest rate by a 
quarter percentage point to a target range of 4.25%-4.5%, marking the lowest level in two years. 
However, FED Chair Jerome Powell and his colleagues revised their 2025 rate-cut expectations, now 
forecasting just two reductions, down from the four previously projected in September. 
U.K. inflation rose to 2.6% in November, marking the second consecutive monthly increase in the 
headline figure. This aligned with economists’ forecasts and was up from 2.3% in October. Core 
inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco, came in at 3.5%, slightly below the 
expected 3.6%, according to a Reuters poll. 
COMMENTARY: Economists had anticipated four rate cuts in 2025, following two reductions this year, 
as inflation eased toward the Bank’s 2% target after the energy-driven price surge.  However, financial 
markets, which recently aligned with this outlook, now expect just two quarter-point cuts due to 
renewed inflationary pressures.

Defying the Odds
WEEKLY EQUITY MARKET OUTLOOK TBC CAPITAL BROKERAGE | 30 DECEMBER 2024
A year ago, the stock market's rally had exceeded all expectations, leaving analysts skeptical about its 
ability to maintain momentum. By the close of 2023, strategists from leading firms like Bank of 
America, Deutsche Bank, and Goldman Sachs predicted a quieter 2024. Following a 20% rise fueled by 
AI advancements and a surprisingly strong economy, the general outlook suggested only modest 
gains for the S&P 500. Many expected bonds to become increasingly competitive as the Federal 
Reserve shifted toward interest rate cuts. 
Contrary to these predictions, the market delivered a stunning performance. By January, the S&P 500 
had already outpaced year-end forecasts, continuing its upward climb throughout the year. Now 
poised for a 25% annual gain, this marks one of the most remarkable back-to-back performances 
since the late 1990s. The unexpected rally left Wall Street experts recalibrating their projections. 
Driving this surge were economic resilience, AI-driven enthusiasm, and massive gains from tech giants 
like Nvidia, Amazon, and Alphabet. Adding to the momentum, Donald Trump’s presidency brought 
promises of tax cuts and policies favorable to businesses. While some, like Morgan Stanley’s Mike 
Wilson, shifted their stance to embrace the bullish trend, others noted the outsized impact of a small 
group of tech leaders. 
Although there are concerns about high valuations and policy risks, the consensus remains optimistic. 
None of Bloomberg’s 19 tracked strategists foresee a decline in 2025. Projections range from stability 
to a 19% rally, with optimism rooted in economic growth and solid corporate performance.

INVESTMENT THEMES
Interesting Road Ahead
WEEKLY EQUITY MARKET OUTLOOK TBC CAPITAL BROKERAGE | 30 DECEMBER 2024
• South Korea’s $1.6 trillion equity market faces 
challenges in 2025, driven by political turmoil, the AI 
boom, and Trump’s presidency. The “Corporate 
Value-Up” campaign pushes governance reforms, 
but impeachment proceedings against President 
Yoon Suk Yeol and a martial law controversy have 
dampened confidence. 
• The Kospi index dropped 8% this year, its worst 
losing streak since 2008, contrasting with an 18% 
global equity rise. Samsung Electronics fell 32% due 
to AI setbacks, weighing on the market, while 
Trump’s trade policies and China’s stimulus efforts 
heightened risks. 
• Bright spots include HD Hyundai Electric, up 370% 
from AI-driven energy demand, and Samyang 
Foods, gaining 250% on U.S. popularity. Banks also 
thrived, buoyed by reform optimism. 
• Conversely, EV battery makers like LG Chem and 
Samsung SDI saw steep losses, falling 50% amid 
weak global demand and policy concerns. Still, 
undervalued stocks and governance improvements 
hint at a potential rebound in 2025.
Travel Boom
• A booming year for US travel has propelled airline 
stocks to exceptional gains, with a bullish outlook 
for 2025. The S&P Supercomposite Airlines Index 
surged 60% in 2024, its best performance since 
2014, outpacing the S&P 500’s 27% rise. United 
Airlines led the pack, soaring 144% and becoming 
one of the S&P 500’s top gainers. 
• Record-breaking travel demand, combined with 
restrained capacity growth—Barclays forecasts seat 
growth below 3% for 2025—has supported this 
rally. Airlines’ cost-cutting efforts, such as reducing 
unprofitable routes, and revamped frequent flyer 
programs have further boosted investor confidence. 
Analysts see strong fundamentals, with legacy 
carriers like United and Delta, as well as Alaska Air 
and Frontier, standing out for their earnings 
potential. 
• Regulatory optimism under President-elect Donald 
Trump, along with raised earnings forecasts from 
JetBlue, Southwest, and American Airlines, adds to 
the sector’s positive momentum.

Supercharged Oil Bets
WEEKLY EQUITY MARKET OUTLOOK TBC CAPITAL BROKERAGE | 30 DECEMBER 2024
• Carlos Slim, Latin America’s wealthiest individual, 
has invested $1 billion this year to expand his crude 
oil production and refining portfolio, reflecting 
confidence in the enduring demand for fossil fuels. 
Known for building the telecom giant América Móvil 
SAB, Slim has diversified into oil, real estate in Spain, 
and a stake in the UK’s BT Group Plc through his 
investment office, Control Empresarial de Capitales. 
Recent investments include $602 million in U.S. 
refiner PBF Energy Inc., raising his stake to 25%, and 
$326 million in Talos Energy Inc., where he now 
owns 24.2%. Slim also increased his share in a 
Mexico joint venture with Talos to 80% for $82.7 
million. Despite these moves, his net worth has 
fallen 22% this year to $81.8 billion due to asset 
declines and a weaker peso. Slim also pledged $1.2 
billion for Mexico’s Lakach offshore gas field 
development, in partnership with Talos and FCC.
China's Property Crisis Continues
• China's property crisis persists as major developers 
face increasing financial strain. Vanke, the country’s 
fourth-largest builder, is under scrutiny for potential 
default risks, with regulators asking insurers to 
assess their exposure to its bonds. Meanwhile, Hong 
Kong-based New World Development is seeking to 
delay loan repayments amid heavy debt, while 
Parkview Group is selling a high-profile Beijing 
commercial complex to reduce costs. 
• Despite government efforts to stabilize the sector, 
including interest rate cuts and state-backed 
guarantees, the property market remains in decline, 
with developers' bonds trading at distressed levels. 
The sector's challenges have spread beyond China, 
with Hong Kong developers also struggling. Vanke’s 
bonds have recently dropped sharply, signaling 
investor concerns over its future, and analysts warn 
of a potential liquidity shortage. While defaults are 
expected to decrease in the coming year, the overall 
property crisis shows few signs of ending soon, with 
further defaults and slow recovery likely.

operated by the joint venture between 
TotalEnergies and EPH.

• Rio Tinto (RIO) has partnered with BHP Group 
(BHP) and BlueScope to develop Australia’s largest 
ironmaking electric smelting furnace (ESF) pilot 
plant in Western Australia. The project will focus on 
processing Pilbara-sourced iron using electric 
furnaces to replace traditional blast furnaces, 
aiming to decarbonize the steelmaking process, 
which contributes to about 8% of global carbon 
emissions. Pending funding, feasibility studies are 
expected to begin in Q2 2025, with the final 
investment decision in 2026 and operations slated 
for 2028.

• Duke Energy (DUK) has filed a $1.1B cost recovery 
plan with the Florida Public Service Commission to 
address expenses incurred during emergency 
responses to hurricanes Debby, Helene, and Milton. 
The costs cover deploying 27,000 workers, 
acquiring mutual assistance, setting up staging 
sites, and replacing critical infrastructure like 1,800 
utility poles damaged by storm surges and winds. 
The restoration effort successfully restored power 
to 2M customers. Residential customers are 
expected to see a ~$21 increase per 1,000 kWh in 
monthly bills starting March 2025. The filing 
highlights the extensive logistical and operational 
challenges faced during hurricane recovery.
